vjimc-2025-cat2-01.title: Contracting differences and an invariant
vjimc-2025-cat2-01.body:
**Convergence.** Let $d_n=x_n-x_{n-1}$ ($n\ge1$). For $n\ge1$,
$$x_{n+4}-x_{n+3}=\frac{x_{n+2}+x_{n+1}}2-\frac{x_{n+1}+x_n}2=\frac{x_{n+2}-x_n}2=\frac12\Big(\frac{x_n+x_{n-1}}2-x_n\Big)=-\frac14(x_n-x_{n-1}),$$
i.e. $d_{n+4}=-\frac14d_n$. Hence $|d_n|\le D\cdot4^{-n/4}$ for all $n\ge1$, where $D=4\max(|d_1|,|d_2|,|d_3|,|d_4|)$, so $\sum|d_n|<\infty$. Thus $x_n=x_0+\sum_{k\le n}d_k$ converges.

**An invariant.** Let $y_n=x_{n+1}+x_n+\frac12x_{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$. Then
$$y_{n+1}=x_{n+2}+x_{n+1}+\tfrac12x_n=\tfrac12x_n+\tfrac12x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}+\tfrac12x_n=x_{n+1}+x_n+\tfrac12x_{n-1}=y_n,$$
so $y_n=y_1=c+b+\frac a2$ for all $n$.

**The limit.** If $x_n\to L$, then $y_n\to L+L+\frac L2=\frac52L$, so $\frac52L=c+b+\frac a2$ and
$$L=\frac{a+2b+2c}{5}.$$
∎

vjimc-2025-cat2-01.title: Characteristic roots
vjimc-2025-cat2-01.body:
The recurrence $x_{k+3}=\frac12x_{k+1}+\frac12x_k$ ($k\ge0$) has characteristic polynomial $2t^3-t-1=(t-1)(2t^2+2t+1)$ with distinct roots $1$ and $\rho,\bar\rho=\frac{-1\pm i}2$, $|\rho|=\frac1{\sqrt2}<1$. Hence $x_k=L+\beta\rho^k+\bar\beta\bar\rho^k$ for some constants, and $x_k\to L$ because $\rho^k\to0$.

To find $L$, let $Q_k=2x_{k+2}+2x_{k+1}+x_k$. Using $2x_{k+3}=x_{k+1}+x_k$,
$$Q_{k+1}=2x_{k+3}+2x_{k+2}+x_{k+1}=(x_{k+1}+x_k)+2x_{k+2}+x_{k+1}=Q_k,$$
so $Q_k$ is constant. With $k=0$ it equals $2c+2b+a$, and in the limit it equals $5L$. So $L=\frac{a+2b+2c}5$. ∎

vjimc-2025-cat2-02.title: Block decomposition along $\operatorname{Im}A\oplus\ker A$
vjimc-2025-cat2-02.body:
The statement is symmetric in $A$ and $B$, so it suffices to show: if $A^{k+1}B^k=A$, then $B^{k+1}A^k=B$. (We take $k\ge1$; for $k=0$ both identities are trivially true.) Let $r=\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$.

**$\ker A=\ker B$.** If $Bx=0$ then $Ax=A^{k+1}B^kx=0$. So $\ker B\subseteq\ker A$, and both have dimension $n-r$; hence they are equal.

**$\mathbb C^n=\operatorname{Im}A\oplus\ker A$.** From $r=\operatorname{rank}(A^{k+1}B^k)\le\operatorname{rank}A^{k+1}\le\operatorname{rank}A^2\le\operatorname{rank}A=r$ we get $\operatorname{rank}A^2=r$, so $\ker A^2$ (which contains $\ker A$) has the same dimension as $\ker A$: $\ker A^2=\ker A$. If $x\in\ker A\cap\operatorname{Im}A$, $x=Ay$, then $A^2y=0$, so $y\in\ker A$ and $x=0$. Since the dimensions add up to $n$, the sum is direct and equals $\mathbb C^n$.

**Block form.** Choose a basis consisting of a basis of $\operatorname{Im}A$ followed by a basis of $\ker A=\ker B$. $A$ maps $\operatorname{Im}A$ into itself, injectively (its kernel meets $\operatorname{Im}A$ trivially), and kills $\ker A$; $B$ kills $\ker A$. Hence
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}B_1&0\\B_3&0\end{pmatrix},$$
with $A_1$ an invertible $r\times r$ matrix. By induction $B^j=\begin{pmatrix}B_1^j&0\\B_3B_1^{j-1}&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $j\ge1$.

**Conclusion.** $A^{k+1}B^k=\begin{pmatrix}A_1^{k+1}B_1^k&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=A$ gives $A_1^{k+1}B_1^k=A_1$, i.e. $A_1^kB_1^k=I_r$ ($A_1$ invertible). Hence $A_1^k$ and $B_1^k$ are inverse to each other, so also $B_1^kA_1^k=I_r$. Now
$$B^{k+1}A^k=\begin{pmatrix}B_1^{k+1}&0\\B_3B_1^k&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A_1^k&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}B_1\,(B_1^kA_1^k)&0\\B_3\,(B_1^kA_1^k)&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}B_1&0\\B_3&0\end{pmatrix}=B .$$
∎

vjimc-2025-cat2-03.title: Substitution $x+1=1/t$
vjimc-2025-cat2-03.body:
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm, and $x^2+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2)$. Substitute $x+1=\frac1t$, $t\in(0,1]$, $dx=-\frac{dt}{t^2}$. Then $x+2=\frac{1+t}t$ and $(x+1)(x+2)=\frac{1+t}{t^2}$, so
$$\int_0^\infty\frac{\ln(x+2)}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx=\int_0^1\ln\frac{1+t}{t}\cdot\frac{t^2}{1+t}\cdot\frac{dt}{t^2}=\int_0^1\frac{\ln(1+t)}{1+t}\,dt-\int_0^1\frac{\ln t}{1+t}\,dt .$$
The first integral is $\big[\frac12\ln^2(1+t)\big]_0^1=\frac12\ln^22$. For the second, expand $\frac1{1+t}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kt^k$ and use $\int_0^1t^k\ln t\,dt=-\frac1{(k+1)^2}$ (termwise integration is justified since the partial sums of the alternating series are bounded by $1$ and $|\ln t|$ is integrable):
$$-\int_0^1\frac{\ln t}{1+t}\,dt=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k}{(k+1)^2}=1-\frac1{4}+\frac19-\dots=\frac{\pi^2}{12}.$$
Hence the integral equals
$$\frac{\pi^2}{12}+\frac{\ln^22}{2}\approx1.062694 .$$
(Numerical integration confirms this value.) ∎

vjimc-2025-cat2-03.title: Differentiation under the integral sign (official approach)
vjimc-2025-cat2-03.body:
Shifting $x\mapsto x-1$, the integral is $I(1)$ where $I(a)=\int_1^\infty\frac{\ln(1+ax)}{x(1+x)}dx$, $I(0)=0$. Differentiating,
$$I'(a)=\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{(1+x)(1+ax)}=\frac1{1-a}\Big[\ln\frac{1+x}{1+ax}\Big]_1^\infty=\frac1{1-a}\Big(\ln\frac1a-\ln\frac2{1+a}\Big)=\frac{\ln\frac{2a}{1+a}}{a-1}.$$
So
$$I(1)=\int_0^1\frac{\ln a}{a-1}\,da+\int_0^1\frac{\ln\frac{1+a}{2}}{1-a}\,da .$$
The first integral is $\sum_{k\ge0}\int_0^1(-\ln a)a^k\,da=\sum\frac1{(k+1)^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6$. In the second, put $1-a=2v$: it becomes $\int_0^{1/2}\frac{\ln(1-v)}{v}dv=-F(\tfrac12)$, where $F(x)=-\int_0^x\frac{\ln(1-v)}v\,dv$. Since $\frac{d}{dx}\big[F(x)+F(1-x)+\ln x\ln(1-x)\big]=0$ on $(0,1)$ and the bracket tends to $F(1)=\frac{\pi^2}6$ as $x\to0^+$, we get $2F(\frac12)+\ln^22=\frac{\pi^2}6$, i.e. $F(\frac12)=\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{\ln^22}2$. Therefore
$$I(1)=\frac{\pi^2}6-\frac{\pi^2}{12}+\frac{\ln^22}2=\frac{\pi^2}{12}+\frac{\ln^22}2 .$$
∎ (The last lines of the official solution sheet contain sign slips; the value above is the correct one.)

vjimc-2025-cat2-04.title: Area with multiplicity (official approach)
vjimc-2025-cat2-04.body:
**Preliminaries.** $f$ is not constant: a constant $c$ with $|c|<1$ violates $|f(z)|\to1$. Since $|f(z)|\to1$ uniformly as $|z|\to1$, for every $\rho<1$ there is $r_0<1$ with $|f(z)|>\rho$ for $r_0<|z|<1$. Hence all zeros of $f$ lie in the compact disk $|z|\le r_0$ (with $\rho=\frac12$), so there are finitely many, say $K$ counted with multiplicity.

**Every $w\in D$ is taken exactly $K$ times.** Fix $w\in D$ and choose $r_0$ as above for $\rho=\frac{1+|w|}2$. For $r\in(r_0,1)$, on $|z|=r$ we have $|(f-w)-f|=|w|<|f|$, so by Rouché's theorem $f-w$ and $f$ have the same number of zeros in $|z|<r$; and neither has zeros in $r_0<|z|<1$ (for $f-w$: $|f|>\rho>|w|$ there). So $f$ takes the value $w$ exactly $K$ times in $D$, counting multiplicity.

**Area computation.** The Jacobian of $z\mapsto f(z)$ as a map of the plane is $|f'(z)|^2$, so by the change-of-variables (area) formula
$$\iint_D|f'(z)|^2\,dA(z)=\iint_D\#\{z\in D:f(z)=w\}\,dA(w)=K\pi ,$$
where the preimages are counted with multiplicity (critical points form a discrete set and do not affect the integral). On the other hand, for $0<r<1$, by orthogonality of $e^{int}$ (Parseval),
$$\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(re^{it})|^2dt=2\pi\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|a_n|^2r^{2n-2},$$
and integrating against $r\,dr$ over $[0,1)$ (monotone convergence),
$$\iint_D|f'|^2\,dA=2\pi\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|a_n|^2\int_0^1r^{2n-1}dr=\pi\sum_{n\ge1}n|a_n|^2 .$$
Comparing, $\sum_{n\ge0}n|a_n|^2=K$, the number of zeros of $f$. ∎

vjimc-2025-cat2-04.title: Blaschke product and the argument principle
vjimc-2025-cat2-04.body:
As in the first solution, $f$ has finitely many zeros $z_1,\dots,z_K$ (with multiplicity), and $K\ge1$ (otherwise $1/f$ would be holomorphic with $|1/f|\to1$ at the boundary, so $|1/f|\le1$ and $|f|\le1$ by the maximum principle, i.e. $|f|=1$ and $f$ constant, impossible).

Let $B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^K\frac{z-z_j}{1-\bar z_jz}$. Each factor is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\overline D$ and has modulus $1$ on $|z|=1$ (since $|z-z_j|=|\bar z-\bar z_j|=|1-\bar z_jz|$ for $|z|=1$), so $|B(z)|\to1$ as $|z|\to1$. Then $g=f/B$ is holomorphic and zero-free on $D$ with $|g(z)|\to1$ as $|z|\to1$. The maximum principle applied to $g$ and to $1/g$ gives $|g|\le1$ and $|1/g|\le1$, so $|g|\equiv1$ and $g\equiv c$ is a unimodular constant. Thus $f=cB$.

$B$ is a rational function whose poles $1/\bar z_j$ lie outside $\overline D$, so the Taylor series of $f$ has radius of convergence $>1$ and converges absolutely on $|z|=1$, as does that of $zf'(z)=\sum na_nz^n$. By Parseval on the unit circle, using $|f|=1$ there (so $\overline{f}=1/f$):
$$\sum_{n\ge0}n|a_n|^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\overline{f(e^{it})}\;e^{it}f'(e^{it})\,dt=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{f'(e^{it})}{f(e^{it})}\,e^{it}\,dt=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\,dz=K,$$
by the argument principle ($f$ has no zeros on $|z|=1$). ∎
